items.en: Removing Bodily Formation: The First Dhyāna
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 除諸身行
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 第五、除諸身行者，對初禪覺觀支。就中二：一、明身行；二、明除身。身行者，欲界身中發得初禪，色界四大造色，觸欲界身，欲界身根生身識，覺此色觸，二界色相依共住，故名身。身行者，即觀支。此觀支從身分生，知身中之法有所造作，故名身行。次明除身行者，因覺息遍身，發得初禪，心眼開明，見身三十六物臭穢可惡，爾時即知三十六物由四大有頭等六分，一一非身，四大之中，各各非身，此即是除欲界身也。
en: Fifth, removing every bodily formation: this corresponds to the first dhyāna's own factor of initial thought and sustained reflection. Within this, there are two parts: clarifying bodily formation; and clarifying the removal of body.

As for bodily formation: the first dhyāna is brought forth within the body of the desire realm, the form realm's own four elements producing form that comes into contact with the desire-realm body — the desire-realm body's own faculty gives rise to body-consciousness, aware of this very tactile contact of form, the two realms' own form dwelling together, dependent on one another — hence this is named "body." "Bodily formation" is precisely the factor of sustained reflection: this factor of sustained reflection arises from the body itself, aware that the dharma within the body has something actually done through it — hence this is named "bodily formation."

Next, clarifying the removal of bodily formation: through perceiving the breath pervading the whole body, the first dhyāna is brought forth, the mind's own eye opening into clarity, seeing the body's thirty-six substances as foul, filthy, and repugnant — at this point, one comes to know that these thirty-six substances, arising from the four elements, are made up of six parts such as the head and the rest, no single one of them being the "body," nor is any single one of the four elements, in itself, the "body" either — this, then, is removing the desire-realm's own body.

zh: 除初禪身者，於欲界身中求色界四大不可得，名除初禪身。所以者何？若言有色界造色者，是為從外來，為從內出，為在中間住？如是觀時，畢竟不可得，但以顛倒憶想，故言受色界觸。諦觀不得，即是除初禪身，身除故，身行即滅。復次，未得初禪時，於欲界身中起種種善惡行，今見身不淨，則不造善惡諸結業，故名除身行。
en: As for removing the first dhyāna's own body: seeking, within the desire-realm body, for the form realm's own four elements, none can be found at all — this is named removing the first dhyāna's own body. Why is this? Were it said that there is form produced by the form realm present, does it come from outside, arise from within, or abide somewhere in between? Contemplating in this way, it can, in the end, never be found at all — it is simply through inverted, deluded thought that one speaks of "receiving the form realm's own tactile contact." Closely contemplated, it cannot be found — this is precisely removing the first dhyāna's own body; the body thus removed, bodily formation is thereby extinguished as well. Furthermore: before the first dhyāna is attained, within the desire-realm body, every kind of wholesome and unwholesome action is given rise to; now, seeing the body as impure, one no longer creates any wholesome or unwholesome karmic bond at all — hence this is named removing bodily formation.

zh: 今明此定亦有二種：一者、根本五支，如前說。二者、淨禪五支者，覺身三十六物虛假不實，名覺；分別此禪與欲界及根本功德大有優劣，名為觀。既得法喜，心大慶悅，名為喜；於無垢受恬憺之樂，名為樂。正定持心，令不動搖，名為一心。此中支除成就勝妙喜樂而心無染著，故名為淨禪也。復次，如《阿毗曇》中說隱沒無記有垢、不隱沒有記無垢等義，約此二種禪中，應廣分別。
en: Here, it is clarified that this concentration is itself likewise of two kinds: the root dhyāna's own five factors, as already described above; and the pure dhyāna's own five factors — perceiving the body's thirty-six substances as empty, provisional, and unreal, this is named initial thought; distinguishing that this dhyāna, the desire realm, and the root dhyāna differ greatly in merit, superior and inferior, this is named sustained reflection; having attained the joy of the Dharma, the mind greatly celebrating and delighted, this is named joy; the tranquil happiness present within this undefiled sensation, this is named happiness; and right concentration sustaining the mind, keeping it from any agitation whatsoever, this is named one-pointedness of mind. Within this, the factors are cleared and brought to accomplishment, excellent, wondrous joy and happiness present while the mind remains free of any defiling attachment — hence this is named the pure dhyāna. Furthermore, as the Abhidharma speaks of the sense of the concealed-and-indeterminate, defiled, versus the unconcealed, determinate, undefiled — with reference to these two kinds of dhyāna, this should be distinguished at length.

"Removing the body" happens in two distinct stages worth keeping separate: first the desire-realm body (dissolved by seeing it as parts, none of which is itself "the body"), then the first dhyāna's own subtler body (dissolved by searching for the form realm's four elements anywhere at all — outside, inside, or in between — and finding nothing). The resulting distinction between a "root" dhyāna and a "pure" dhyāna, sharing the same five factors but differing in whether contemplative wisdom accompanies them, gives a precise technical answer to what has been implicit throughout fascicle 5: the very same factor-structure can be either an ordinary, defiled attainment or a pure one, depending entirely on whether insight is layered on top of it.

items.en: Receiving Joy, Happiness, and Mental Formations
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 受喜、受樂、受諸心行
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 六、受喜者，即是對破初禪喜支。根本禪中喜支從隱沒有垢，覺觀後生，既無觀慧照了，多生煩惱，故不應受。今明受喜者，於淨禪覺觀支中生，以有觀行破析，達覺觀性空，當知從覺觀生喜亦空，即於喜中不著，無諸過罪，故說受喜。如羅漢人不著一切供養，故名應供。復次，如真實知見，得真法喜，故說受喜。七、受樂者，對根本禪樂支。彼禪既無觀慧，樂中多染，故不應受。今言受樂者，受無樂，知樂性空，於樂中不著。既無樂過罪，上無別證無為之樂，故說受樂。
en: Sixth, receiving joy: this corresponds to, and breaks through, the first dhyāna's own factor of joy. Within the root dhyāna, the factor of joy arises from the concealed, defiled factors of initial thought and sustained reflection, arising afterward — and, there being no contemplative wisdom to illuminate it, this, for the most part, gives rise to affliction, and so ought not to be received. Here, what is clarified as receiving joy arises instead from the pure dhyāna's own factor of initial thought and sustained reflection, and, through contemplative practice analyzing and breaking through it, one penetrates the very emptiness of initial thought and sustained reflection's own nature — one should thereby know that the joy arising from initial thought and sustained reflection is likewise empty, and so is no longer clung to within this very joy, free of every fault — hence this is called receiving joy. It is like an arhat who no longer clings to any offering whatsoever, and so is named "worthy of offerings." Furthermore: through this true knowledge and vision, one attains the true joy of the Dharma itself — hence this is called receiving joy.

Seventh, receiving happiness: this corresponds to the root dhyāna's own factor of happiness. That dhyāna, lacking any contemplative wisdom at all, its happiness, for the most part, defiled — and so ought not to be received. Here, what is spoken of as receiving happiness means receiving a happiness that is itself without happiness — knowing happiness's own nature to be empty, and so no longer clinging to it within happiness itself. Free of happiness's own fault in this way, and yet without any further, separately realized unconditioned happiness above it either — hence this is called receiving happiness.

zh: 八、受諸心行者，此對破根本一心支。今明能通諸法，故名諸心行。心行有二種：一者、動行；二者、不動行。有人解云：從初禪乃至三禪猶是動行，四禪已去，名不動行。今略說不動行者，覺等四支是動行，後一心支是不動行。亦名諸心行者，即是一心支不動之行。若根本禪入一心時，心生染著，此一心不應受。今明受諸心行者，知此一心虛誑不實，一心非心，即不取著，既無過罪，即是三昧正受，故說受諸心行。
en: Eighth, receiving every mental formation: this corresponds to, and breaks through, the root dhyāna's own factor of one-pointedness of mind. Here, what is clarified as being able to pervade every dharma is named "every mental formation." Mental formation is itself of two kinds: moving formation; and unmoving formation. Some explain: from the first dhyāna all the way through the third, this is still moving formation; from the fourth dhyāna onward, it is named unmoving formation. Here, briefly speaking of unmoving formation: the preceding four factors, initial thought and the rest, are moving formation, while the last, the factor of one-pointedness of mind, is unmoving formation. This, too, is what is meant by "every mental formation": precisely the unmoving formation of the factor of one-pointedness of mind itself.

Within the root dhyāna, at the moment one-pointedness of mind is entered, a mind of defiling attachment arises — this one-pointedness of mind ought not to be received. Here, what is clarified as receiving every mental formation means knowing this very one-pointedness of mind to be deceptive and unreal, this one-pointedness of mind itself not truly "mind" at all, and so no longer grasping or clinging to it — and, being thereby free of any fault, this is itself the true reception of samādhi — hence this is called receiving every mental formation.

Items six through eight complete the first dhyāna's own five-factor structure (initial thought and sustained reflection already handled by item five) by showing that "receiving" joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind in the special-excellences sense is almost the opposite of ordinary reception — it means seeing each factor's own emptiness clearly enough that clinging becomes impossible, "a happiness that is itself without happiness." The arhat simile (no longer clinging to any offering, and so uniquely "worthy" of them) captures the paradox precisely: freedom from attachment to a good thing is what actually allows it to be received purely.

items.en: The Second and Third Dhyānas: Joy, Restraint, and Liberation
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 心作喜、心作攝、心住解脫
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 九、心作喜者，此對二禪內淨喜。所以者何？二禪喜從內淨發，以無智慧照了多受也。今觀此喜，即知虛誑不生受著，如真實知生法喜，亦名喜覺分。既從正觀，心生真法喜，故名心作喜。十、心作攝者，此對二禪一心支。何以故？為二禪喜動經攝，故說心作攝。今明攝者，正以破前偽喜，生喜覺喜，此喜雖正，而不無湧動之過，即應返觀喜性。既知空寂畢竟，定心不亂，不隨喜動，故云作攝。是以《大集經》云：「動至心。」
en: Ninth, the mind making joy: this corresponds to the second dhyāna's own inner-purity joy. Why is this? The second dhyāna's own joy arises from inner purity, and, lacking any wisdom to illuminate it, is, for the most part, received with attachment. Here, contemplating this very joy, one comes to know it as deceptive and false, and so does not give rise to any attached reception of it — and, through this true knowledge, one gives rise instead to the true joy of the Dharma, also named the factor of enlightenment that is joy. Arising, in this way, from right contemplation, the mind gives rise to the true joy of the Dharma — hence this is named the mind making joy.

Tenth, the mind making restraint: this corresponds to the second dhyāna's own factor of one-pointedness of mind. Why is this? Because the second dhyāna's own joy, once stirred, must be gathered back in through restraint — hence this is called the mind making restraint. Here, what is clarified as "restraint" is precisely breaking through the previous, false joy, giving rise instead to the joy of the factor of enlightenment. Though this joy is itself correct, it is nonetheless not entirely without the fault of an excited, surging movement — one should therefore turn the contemplation back upon the very nature of this joy. Knowing it, in the end, to be empty and still, the concentrated mind remains undisturbed, no longer following this excited movement of joy — hence this is called making restraint. Hence the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "Movement, brought all the way to the very mind itself."

zh: 十一、心住解脫者，此對破三禪樂。所以者何？三禪有遍身之樂，凡夫得之，多生染愛，為之所縛，不得解脫。今言解脫者，以觀慧破析，證遍身樂時，即知此樂從因緣生，空無自性，虛誑不實，觀樂不著，心得自在，故名心作解脫。
en: Eleventh, the mind abiding in liberation: this corresponds to, and breaks through, the third dhyāna's own happiness. Why is this? The third dhyāna has happiness pervading the whole body present within it; an ordinary person, attaining it, for the most part gives rise to defiled attachment, bound by it, unable to attain liberation. Here, what is spoken of as liberation means that, through contemplative wisdom analyzing and breaking through it, at the very moment this pervasive happiness is realized, one knows this happiness to arise from causes and conditions, empty, without any nature of its own, deceptive and unreal — contemplating happiness without clinging to it, the mind attains freedom — hence this is named the mind making liberation.

Item ten's "restraint" is a subtle refinement worth flagging: it is not restraint of the second dhyāna's original, false joy (already broken through by item nine's "making joy"), but restraint of the correct, wisdom-born joy that item nine itself produced — the treatise catching an excess in its own antidote before it can become a new attachment in turn. This is the same pattern already seen with the six wondrous gates' own escalating dissatisfaction (each stage revealing the next as too coarse by comparison), now applied one level deeper, to a state that is already correct rather than merely false.

items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 觀無常
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 十二、觀無常，此對破四禪不動。所以者何？如世間中有動、有不動法，三種為樂所動，猶名動法。今此四禪名不動定，凡夫得此定時，多生常想，心生愛取，今若觀此定生滅代謝，三相所遷，知是破壞不安之相，故經云：「一切世間動、不動法皆敗壞不安之相。」故名觀無常。
en: Twelfth, contemplating impermanence: this corresponds to, and breaks through, the fourth dhyāna's own unmoving concentration. Why is this? Just as, within the mundane world, there are dharmas both moving and unmoving — the three lower dhyānas, moved by happiness, are still named "moving" dharmas. This fourth dhyāna, by contrast, is named the unmoving concentration; an ordinary person, attaining this concentration, for the most part gives rise to a notion of permanence, the mind giving rise to craving and grasping. Here, however, contemplating that this very concentration arises, ceases, and passes through change, shifted by the three marks of conditioned existence, one knows it to bear the very mark of destruction and instability — hence the sūtra says: "Every dharma in the mundane world, whether moving or unmoving, bears the mark of destruction and instability alike." Hence this is named contemplating impermanence.

This item's whole force rests on the fourth dhyāna's own name — "unmoving" — being exactly the trap that catches an ordinary practitioner: mistaking the absence of gross agitation for the absence of impermanence itself. The sūtra citation makes the correction precise: "moving" and "unmoving" describe only a dharma's own internal turbulence, not whether it is subject to arising and ceasing at all — even the most stable-feeling attainment in the entire mundane hierarchy is still, at bottom, "shifted by the three marks of conditioned existence."

items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 觀出散、觀離欲、觀滅
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 十三、觀出散者，此對破空處。所以者何？出者，即是出離色界；散者，即是散三種色。復次，出散者，謂出離色心，依虛空消散自在，不為色法所縛，故名出散。凡夫得此定時，謂是真空安隱，心生取著。今言觀出散者，行人初入虛空處時，即知四陰和合故有，無自性，不可取著。所以者何？若言有出散者，為虛空是出散，為心是出散？若心出散，心為三相所遷，過去已謝，未來未至，現在無住，何能出耶？若空是出散者，空是無知，無知之法，有何出散？既不得空定，則心無受著，是名觀出散。
en: Thirteenth, contemplating dispersal: this corresponds to, and breaks through, the sphere of space. Why is this? "Leaving" here means leaving the form realm behind; "dispersing" means dispersing the three kinds of form. Furthermore, "leaving and dispersal" means leaving both form and mind behind, relying instead on empty space's own dissolution and freedom, no longer bound by the dharma of form — hence this is named leaving and dispersal. An ordinary person, attaining this concentration, takes it to be a true, secure emptiness, the mind giving rise to grasping and attachment.

Here, what is spoken of as contemplating dispersal means that the practitioner, upon first entering the sphere of space, already knows that this exists only through the combining together of the four aggregates, without any nature of its own, and so cannot properly be grasped or clung to. Why is this? Were it said that there is genuinely something that "disperses" here, is it empty space itself that disperses, or is it the mind that disperses? If it is the mind that disperses, the mind is itself shifted by the three marks of conditioned existence — the past already gone, the future not yet arrived, and the present never remaining still — how, then, could it possibly "leave" at all? And if it is space itself that disperses, space is itself without any knowing at all — how could a dharma without any knowing possibly "disperse"? Since the concentration of emptiness can thus never actually be found, the mind is thereby free of any attached reception of it — this is named contemplating dispersal.

zh: 十四、觀離欲者，此對識處。所以者何？一切愛著外境，皆名為欲。從欲界乃至空處，皆是心外之境。若虛空為外境，識來領受此空，即以空為所欲。今識處定緣於內識，能離外空欲故離欲。若凡夫得此定，無慧眼照了，謂言心與識法相應，真實安隱，即生染著。今言觀離欲者得此定時，即觀破析。若言以心緣識，心與識相應，得入定者，此實不然。何以故？過去、未來、現在三世識皆不與現在心相應故，云何言心與三世識相應？定法持心，名為識定。故知此識定但有名字，虛誑不實，故名離欲也。
en: Fourteenth, contemplating freedom from desire: this corresponds to the sphere of consciousness. Why is this? Every attachment to an external object whatsoever is named "desire." From the desire realm all the way through the sphere of space, all of it is an object external to the mind. If empty space itself is taken as an external object, and consciousness comes to receive this very emptiness, then emptiness itself is taken as an object of desire. Here, the concentration of the sphere of consciousness takes internal consciousness as its object, and is thereby able to leave the desire for external emptiness behind — hence it is named freedom from desire.

An ordinary person, attaining this concentration, lacking the wisdom-eye to illuminate it, takes it that the mind corresponds with the dharma of consciousness itself, truly and genuinely secure, and so gives rise to defiled attachment. Here, what is spoken of as contemplating freedom from desire means that, upon attaining this concentration, one contemplates it, analyzing and breaking through it directly. Were it said that the mind takes consciousness as its object, the mind corresponding with consciousness, and thereby enters concentration — this is, in truth, not so at all. Why is this? Because the consciousness of the past, future, and present, across all three periods of time, never actually corresponds with the present mind at all — how, then, could it be said that the mind corresponds with the consciousness of the three periods of time? The dharma of concentration sustains the mind — this is named the concentration of consciousness. Hence it is known that this concentration of consciousness has only a name, deceptive and unreal — hence it is named freedom from desire.

zh: 十五、觀滅者，此對無所有處。所以者何？此定緣無為法塵，心與無為相應。對無為法塵發少識故，凡夫得之，謂之心滅，深生愛著，不能捨，為之所縛。今言觀滅者，得此定時，即覺有少識。此識雖少，亦有四陰和合，無常、無我、虛誑，譬如糞穢，多少俱臭，不可染著，是名觀滅。
en: Fifteenth, contemplating cessation: this corresponds to the sphere of nothingness. Why is this? This concentration takes the unconditioned dharma-object as its object, the mind corresponding with the unconditioned. In response to this unconditioned dharma-object, only a slight consciousness is brought forth — an ordinary person, attaining this, takes it that the mind itself has ceased, giving rise to deep attachment, unable to relinquish it, bound by it. Here, what is spoken of as contemplating cessation means that, upon attaining this concentration, one becomes aware directly that a slight consciousness is nonetheless still present. Though this consciousness is slight, it, too, is made up of the four aggregates combining together, impermanent, without self, deceptive — like filth and excrement, whether much or little, equally foul — not to be attached to or clung to at all. This is named contemplating cessation.

Items thirteen through fifteen repeat, at the formless level, the exact critique fascicle 6 already made of each of these same three spheres — but the special excellences add a distinctive analytic move at item thirteen worth isolating: asking not just "is this attainment empty?" but "what, grammatically, would even be doing the dispersing?" and finding neither space (which has no knowing to disperse) nor mind (which, being already in flux across the three time-periods, has no fixed state to disperse from) can coherently fill that role. This is a sharper, more explicitly logical register than the parallel passages in fascicle 6, consistent with these items being contemplative wisdom retracing concentration's own prior ground.

items.en: Relinquishment, Subhadra, and the Closing Summary
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 觀棄捨、結歎
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 十六、觀棄捨者，此對非想。所以者何？非想是兩捨之對治，從初禪以來，但有遍捨，無有兩捨，故未與棄捨之名。今此非想既有雙捨有無，故名棄捨。亦以此定是捨中之極，故最後受名。若凡夫得此定時，謂為涅槃，無有觀慧覺了，不能捨離。今明棄捨者，得此定時，即知四陰、十二入、三界及十種細心數等和合所成。當知此定無常、苦、空、無我，虛誑不實，不應計為涅槃，生安樂想。既知空寂，即不受著，是名觀棄捨。
en: Sixteenth, contemplating relinquishment: this corresponds to neither perception nor non-perception. Why is this? Neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the antidote to a double relinquishment; from the first dhyāna onward, there has only been a single, general relinquishment at each stage, never a double relinquishment — and so the name "relinquishment" has not yet been given until now. Here, this very state of neither perception nor non-perception involves relinquishing both existence and nonexistence together — hence it is named relinquishment. It is also because this concentration is the very utmost point of relinquishment that it receives this name last of all.

An ordinary person, attaining this concentration, takes it to be nirvāṇa itself, lacking any contemplative wisdom to illuminate it, unable to relinquish and leave it behind. Here, what is clarified as relinquishment means that, upon attaining this concentration, one knows directly that it is made up of the combining together of the four aggregates, the twelve sense-bases, the three realms, and the ten kinds of subtle mental factors. One should know that this concentration is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, deceptive and unreal, not to be reckoned as nirvāṇa, nor should any notion of peace and happiness be given rise to regarding it. Knowing it to be empty and still in this way, one no longer receives or clings to it — this is named contemplating relinquishment.

zh: 雖求定相，而亦成就此定，爾時即具二種棄捨：一者、根本棄捨；二者、涅槃棄捨。永棄生死，故云觀棄捨。行者爾時深觀棄捨，即便得悟三乘涅槃。此事如須跋陀羅，佛令觀非想中細想，即便獲得阿羅漢果。今明悟道未必應須具十六，或得三二特勝，即便得悟。亦利根者，初隨息時，覺悟無常，即便悟道。此隨人不定也。從初以來，俱發根本定，故名亦有漏；於中觀行，破析不著，名亦無漏。故云特勝是亦有漏亦無漏禪。此竪對三界諸禪者，則一一觀法相，至義可見也。
釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第七
en: Although one seeks the mark of this very concentration, and does indeed accomplish it, at this point one is complete with two kinds of relinquishment at once: the root relinquishment; and the relinquishment of nirvāṇa itself. Forever relinquishing birth-and-death — hence this is called contemplating relinquishment.

The practitioner, at this point, deeply contemplating relinquishment, thereby comes to awaken to the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles directly. This matter is exactly as with Subhadra: the Buddha had him contemplate the subtle perception present within neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and he thereby attained the fruit of arhatship at once.

Here, it is clarified that awakening to the path need not necessarily require all sixteen items in full — one may attain awakening through only two or three of the special excellences alone. Likewise, a practitioner of sharp faculty may, already at the very first stage of following the breath, awaken to impermanence and thereby awaken to the path directly — this differs, and is not fixed, from person to person.

From the very outset, these all bring forth the root concentrations alike — hence they, too, are named contaminated; and, within them, the contemplative practice analyzing and breaking through, without clinging to anything — hence they, too, are named uncontaminated. Hence it is said that the special excellences are dhyāna that is both contaminated and uncontaminated at once. As for this vertical correspondence to the various dhyānas across the three realms, the mark of each single contemplative method, down to its very sense, may be seen throughout.
Shi Chan Boluomi Cidi Famen, Fascicle Seven, ends here.

Subhadra was traditionally the Buddha's very last personal convert before his parinirvāṇa — invoking him here, at the close of the sixteenth and final special excellence, gives this whole method a kind of bookend authority: the same contemplation that opened with the Buddha's own practice beneath the bodhi tree (echoed throughout this fascicle's account of the six wondrous gates) closes with the very last person the Buddha personally taught. The explicit statement that awakening "need not necessarily require all sixteen items in full" is worth holding onto against the sheer length of this fascicle's own exposition — the sixteen-fold structure is a complete map of the territory, not sixteen mandatory checkpoints every practitioner must pass through in sequence. This closes the sixteen special excellences, and with them, fascicle 7 in its entirety — dhyāna both mundane and world-transcending's first two named practices now complete, with the thorough-and-bright contemplation, the third, still to come.

quiz.q: How is the desire-realm body removed?
options: seeing the thirty-six substances as foul, one knows the six parts from the four elements are each not the body
by rebirth in the form realm
quiz.why: Seeing the thirty-six substances as foul, one knows they form six parts such as the head, none of which is the body, nor is any element; this removes the desire-realm body.

quiz.q: How is the first dhyāna's body removed?
options: seeking the form realm's elements in the desire-realm body, from outside, within, or between, they cannot be found
quiz.why: Seeking the form realm's elements within the desire-realm body, whether from outside, within, or between, they can never be found; this removes the first dhyāna's body.

quiz.q: In the pure dhyāna's five factors, what is sustained reflection?
options: perceiving the thirty-six substances as unreal
distinguishing that this dhyāna differs greatly in merit from the desire realm and the root dhyāna
quiz.why: Sustained reflection is distinguishing this dhyāna's merit from the desire realm and root dhyāna. B is initial thought, C joy, D one-pointedness.

quiz.q: In receiving joy, what is the arhat compared to?
options: an arhat clings to no offering and so is worthy of offerings; likewise one receives joy without clinging
an arhat in the root first dhyāna
quiz.why: Seeing the joy born of thought and reflection as empty, one does not cling to it, just as an arhat clings to no offering and is therefore worthy of offerings.

quiz.q: Why should the root dhyāna's happiness not be received, and what is receiving happiness in the excellences?
options: the root dhyāna lacks contemplative wisdom and its happiness is defiled; in the excellences one receives a happiness without happiness, knowing its nature empty
quiz.why: The root dhyāna lacks contemplative wisdom, so its happiness is mostly defiled; receiving happiness here means receiving it as empty and not clinging.

quiz.q: In receiving every mental formation, how does the text briefly distinguish moving and unmoving formation?
options: first to third dhyāna moving, fourth onward unmoving
initial thought and the other three factors are moving; one-pointedness is unmoving
quiz.why: Some say the first three dhyānas are moving and the fourth onward unmoving (option B); the text's own brief account makes the four factors from initial thought moving and one-pointedness unmoving.

quiz.q: How does the joy of "the mind making joy" differ from the root second dhyāna's joy?
options: the root joy is received with attachment; here, seeing it as false, true Dharma-joy arises, the enlightenment factor of joy
quiz.why: The second dhyāna's joy arises from inner purity but, without wisdom, is clung to; contemplating it as false, one gives rise to true Dharma-joy, the enlightenment factor of joy.

quiz.q: What in the third dhyāna does "abiding in liberation" break through, and how?
options: the body-pervading happiness; knowing it arises from conditions, empty, one does not cling and the mind is free
quiz.why: Ordinary people are bound by the third dhyāna's body-pervading happiness; seeing it arise from conditions, empty and unreal, one does not cling, and the mind is free.

quiz.q: Why is contemplating impermanence used against the fourth dhyāna?
options: the unmoving concentration leads ordinary people to imagine permanence; seeing it arise, cease, and change reveals its instability
quiz.why: The fourth dhyāna is called unmoving, so ordinary people imagine it permanent; contemplating its arising, ceasing, and change reveals instability. The lower three, moved by happiness, are still "moving."

quiz.q: Why is contemplating freedom from desire, matched to the sphere of consciousness, so named?
options: all attachment to external objects is desire; up to the sphere of space all are external; consciousness takes inner consciousness and leaves the desire for outer space
quiz.why: Every attachment to an external object is "desire"; everything through the sphere of space is external; the sphere of consciousness takes inner consciousness and leaves desire for outer space behind.

quiz.q: In contemplating cessation, what simile shows that even a slight consciousness should not be clung to?
options: like excrement, foul whether much or little
quiz.why: Even the slight consciousness is the four aggregates combined, impermanent and without self, like excrement that is foul whether much or little.

quiz.q: Why is the name "relinquishment" given only at neither perception nor non-perception?
options: earlier stages have only a single relinquishment; this one relinquishes both existence and nonexistence and is the utmost, so it is named last
quiz.why: From the first dhyāna on there was only a single relinquishment; this state relinquishes both existence and nonexistence and is the utmost relinquishment, so it is named last.

quiz.q: What does the example of Subhadra show, and must all sixteen be completed to awaken?
options: contemplating the subtle perception in that state he became an arhat; not all sixteen are needed, and the sharp may awaken at the first stage
quiz.why: The Buddha had Subhadra contemplate the subtle perception in that state and he became an arhat; awakening need not require all sixteen, and the sharp may awaken already when following the breath.
